Personalized Competitive Programming Difficulty and Skill-Gap Estimator¶

ES 335 Machine Learning, IIT Gandhinagar, 2026. Sarthak Saini (26120007) and Aditya Anup Dhomne (26120001).

Question. Can classical machine-learning models estimate the probability that a Codeforces user will solve a programming problem from their rating, previous contest performance, submission history, the problem's difficulty and its tags? And can these predictions identify a user's weak topics and recommend problems at an appropriate difficulty?

Unit and target. One row is one user–problem interaction, created at the user's first solo submission to that problem (the prediction point). The target is 1 if the user gets an accepted submission on that problem within 30 days of that first attempt, else 0. Every feature uses only events strictly before the prediction point.

This notebook runs the steps in src/ one at a time and shows the evidence. python -m src.pipeline runs the same steps headlessly.

1. Data¶

Collected from the public Codeforces API (user.ratedList, user.info, user.rating, user.status, problemset.problems) by src/collect.py: 80 rated users from each of five rating bands, with complete submission histories. No login or API key is involved.

build() turns submissions into interactions, computes point-in-time features and makes the chronological split. Only rated problems are kept, because difficulty is central to the question and to recommendations, and an interaction is kept only if its full 30-day outcome window is observed before the data ends.

3. Features and leakage control¶

src/features.py replays each user's history in time order. For every interaction it computes features from events strictly before the first attempt; events in the same second do not see each other. The 47 features are:

  • Rating and contest performance: user rating before the attempt (1400 if unrated, plus an is_rated flag), maximum rating, number of rated contests, last rating change, mean of the last five changes, days since the last contest.
  • Difficulty: problem rating, rating gap, and the Elo expected score 1 / (1 + 10^(gap/400)).
  • Submission history: problems attempted so far, smoothed solve rate, problems attempted in the last 30 days, days active, smoothed solve rate on problems within ±200 rating points.
  • Topic history: the user's smoothed solve rate on the problem's tags (mean, minimum, relative to overall) and their experience with the least-practised tag.
  • Problem tags: 25 binary indicators for tags on at least 2% of catalog problems, and the participation mode.

Solve rates use Beta(1, 1) smoothing so that one lucky solve does not count as 100%. A problem that was attempted but not yet solved counts as unsolved as of that moment. That is what was known then, not a final failure. Unattempted problems never enter the data, so missing submissions are never treated as failures. tests/test_features.py checks that adding future submissions does not change past features.

Chronological split. Cut points are row quantiles of attempt time: train before 4 Jan 2025, validation until 25 Oct 2025, test after. An earlier row is kept only if its 30-day outcome window closes before the next period starts, so no training label depends on events in a later period. This embargo drops 7,383 rows.

4. Baselines and candidate models¶

  • Baseline (rating gap): the Elo expected score from the user–problem rating difference, the rule from our proposal. Nothing is learned from our data. It is a meaningful baseline because it uses the strongest single pattern (relative difficulty) and represents rating-based selection.
  • Logistic Regression: additive in log-odds after standardisation, so it's interpretable. C is tuned.
  • Random Forest: bagged deep trees that capture non-linear effects and interactions. Depth and leaf size are tuned.
  • Gradient Boosting (scikit-learn HistGradientBoostingClassifier): sequential trees that capture interactions such as difficulty mattering differently by experience. Learning rate and tree size are tuned.

Every configuration is fitted on training rows and compared by validation ROC-AUC. The best configuration of each family is then refitted on train + validation and scored once on test.

5. Test evaluation¶

Metrics (as taught in Lectures 6, 9 and 10). ROC-AUC is the area under the ROC curve: the share of (solved, unsolved) pairs the model orders correctly. Accuracy misleads when one class is rare, and here only 5.7% of test rows are unsolved, so we report precision, recall and F1 for the "not solved" class. These use a threshold on P(not solved) chosen to maximise F1 on validation and frozen before testing. Binary cross-entropy (log loss) and a calibration plot check the quality of the probabilities.

Gradient Boosting leads on validation and test. Random Forest is statistically indistinguishable from it (the interval for the difference includes zero), and both clearly beat Logistic Regression and the rating-gap baseline. Predicting "solved" for everything would already be 94.3% accurate while flagging nothing, so accuracy is the wrong metric here. Gradient Boosting's flags are right 32.8% of the time, about 5.8 times the 5.7% base rate, and it catches 29.4% of unsolved problems. The baseline ranks reasonably but its probabilities are far off (cross-entropy 1.07 against 0.18), because the Elo formula predicts winning a head-to-head contest, not finishing a problem within a month. The selected model's probabilities are well calibrated in every bin.

Two thirds of confident misses are practice attempts, where nothing forces a user to finish what they open; the sampled examples are experienced users on problems a little above their level. The sampled surprises are problems well above the user's rating that were solved anyway. By far the most useful feature is the user's own solve rate at similar difficulty, followed by participation mode and the Elo expectation.

7. Topic-wise skill gaps and recommendations¶

Skill gap. For a user at a given moment, take unattempted catalog problems within −100 to +300 of their rating. For each tag, compare the model's probability using the user's real topic record with the probability after replacing that record by their overall record. Because small per-topic samples are smoothed toward 50%, raw differences lean negative for everyone, so we centre each user's gaps on their average topic. Negative then means a relative weakness. A topic that is hard for everyone does not show up as a gap.

Does it hold up? At the start of the test period we flag each user's three weakest and three strongest topics, then look at what actually happened. To control for difficulty and general skill, we use residuals against the same model trained without any topic-history features.

Recommendations. Candidates are ranked by predicted solve probability among problems at or above the user's rating ("stretch" problems). We test whether this ranking orders each user's real stretch attempts in the test period better than the simple rule of taking the problems closest to their rating first.

Skill gaps. Topics flagged weak were solved less often in the test period than topics flagged strong (89.2% against 93.9%). But once difficulty and general ability are accounted for, the difference shrinks to −1.3 points with an interval that includes zero. Removing the topic-history features also leaves test ROC-AUC unchanged. We therefore present skill gaps as a descriptive summary of a user's record, not as a validated prediction. This is a negative result, and we report it as one.

Recommendations. On stretch problems, the model's ranking separates solved from unsolved better than "closest rating first" (mean per-user AUC 0.655 against 0.622; the 95% interval for the difference, +0.001 to +0.065, excludes zero). Its top five picks per user were also much harder (274 points above the user on average, against 81) and were solved slightly more often (90.1% against 88.8%). Personalised selection finds harder problems the user will still finish. This is an offline check on problems users chose themselves, not a controlled experiment.

9. Limitations¶

  • Self-selection. We only see problems people chose to attempt, which is why 94% are solved. Estimates for problems far from a user's usual choices are extrapolations.
  • Sample. 400 rated users balanced by rating band, not a random sample of Codeforces. Prolific users contribute many more rows.
  • Snapshot metadata. Problem ratings and tags were fetched in 2026. Older attempts may have seen different values, and the rating itself is partly derived from how many people solved the problem.
  • Target definition. "Solved within 30 days" ignores effort: a solve after 20 wrong submissions counts the same as a first-try solve.
  • Skill gaps did not show predictive value beyond overall skill and difficulty. Recommendations were evaluated offline on users' own choices, not in a controlled experiment.
  • Time shift. Test covers Oct 2025 to Oct 2026. Behaviour (for example, AI-assisted solving) may change over time and change these relationships.
